question.text: A nucleus has mass number $\alpha$ and radius $R_{\alpha}$. Another nucleus has mass number $\beta$ and radius $R_{\beta}$. If $\beta=8 \alpha$ then $R_{\alpha} / R_{\beta}$ is:

solution.text:
Nuclear radius follows $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$ where $A$ is mass number.
Given $\beta = 8\alpha$, we have $R_\alpha = R_0 \alpha^{1/3}$ and $R_\beta = R_0 (8\alpha)^{1/3} = R_0 \cdot 2 \alpha^{1/3} = 2R_\alpha$.
Thus $R_\alpha/R_\beta = 1/2 = 0.5$.

question.text: Which of the following pair of nuclei are isobars of the element?

solution.text:
Isobars are atoms of different chemical elements that have the same number of nucleons (mass number $A$), but different atomic numbers ($Z$).
In the given options:
(1) $_1^3\text{H}$ and $_2^3\text{He}$: Both have the same mass number $A = 3$. Since they have different atomic numbers ($Z=1$ and $Z=2$), they are isobars.
(2) $_1^2\text{H}$ and $_1^3\text{H}$: These have the same atomic number ($Z=1$) but different mass numbers. They are isotopes.
(3) $_{80}^{198}\text{Hg}$ and $_{79}^{197}\text{Au}$: These have different mass numbers ($198$ and $197$).
(4) $_{92}^{236}\text{U}$ and $_{92}^{238}\text{U}$: These have the same atomic number ($Z=92$) but different mass numbers. They are isotopes.
Thus, the pair $_1^3\text{H}$ and $_2^3\text{He}$ are isobars.

question.text: $7.9 \mathrm{MeV} \alpha$-particle scatters from a target material of atomic number 79. From the given data the estimated diameter of nuclei of the target material is (approximately) $\_\_\_\_$ m. $\left[\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{\mathrm{o}}}=9 \times 10^{9} \mathrm{Nm}^{2} / \mathrm{C}^{2}\right.$ and electron charge $\left.=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}\right]$

solution.text:
For Rutherford scattering, at the closest approach all kinetic energy converts to electrostatic potential energy.
For alpha particle-nucleus collision:
$K.E. = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Z_1 Z_2 e^2}{r_{min}}$
Where: $Z_1 = 2$ (alpha), $Z_2 = 79$ (gold), $K.E. = 7.9$ MeV
$r_{min} = \frac{9 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 79 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{7.9 \times 10^6 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}$
$r_{min} = 2.88 \times 10^{-14}$ m
The estimated nuclear diameter is approximately:
$d = 2 \times r_{min} = 5.76 \times 10^{-14}$ m

question.text: For a nucleus of mass number $A$ and radius $R$, the mass density of nucleus can be represented as

solution.text:
The mass density ( $\rho$) of a nucleus is defined as the ratio of its mass to its volume:
$\rho=$ Mass of nucleus / Volume of nucleus
For a spherical nucleus with radius R , the volume is:
$\text { Volume }=(4 / 3) \pi R^3$
The mass of the nucleus is related to the mass number A :
$\text { Mass }-\mathrm{A} \times \mathrm{m} \text { _u }$
(where m_u is the atomic mass unit, approximately $1.66 \times 10^{-27} \mathrm{~kg}$)
Therefore:
$\rho=\left(\mathrm{A} \times \mathrm{m} \_\mathrm{u}\right) /\left[(4 / 3) \pi \mathrm{R}^3\right]$
Now, there's an important relationship between the mass number A and nuclear radius R. Empirically, it has been found that:
$\mathrm{R}=\mathrm{Ro} * \mathrm{~A}^{\wedge}(1 / 3)$
Where Ro is a constant approximately equal to $1.2 \times 10^{-15} \mathrm{~m}(1.2$ fermi).
Substituting this into the density equation:
$\begin{aligned}
& \rho=\left(\mathrm{A} \times \mathrm{m} \_\mathrm{u}\right) /\left[(4 / 3) \pi\left(\mathrm{Ro} \times \mathrm{A}^{\wedge}(1 / 3)\right)^3\right] \\ & \rho=(\mathrm{A} \times \mathrm{m} \text { _u }) /\left[(4 / 3) \pi \mathrm{Ro}^3 \times \mathrm{A}\right] \\ & \rho=\mathrm{m} \_\mathrm{u} /\left[(4 / 3) \pi \mathrm{Ro}^3\right]
\end{aligned}$
This shows that the nuclear density is approximately constant for all nuclei, regardless of their mass number. This is a fundamental property of nuclear matter known as nuclear saturation density.
The numerical value is:
$\rho=2.3 \times 10^{17} \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^3$

question.text: The energy released if hydrogen atoms are combined to form $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ is __________ MeV. (Take binding energies per nucleon of $^{2}_{1}\text{H}$ and $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ as $1.1$ MeV and $7.2$ MeV, respectively)

solution.text:
The fusion reaction is given by:

$2 ^{2}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow ^{4}_{2}\text{He}$

Binding energy of one $^{2}_{1}\text{H}$ nucleus = $2 \times 1.1 = 2.2$ MeV

Total initial binding energy = $2 \times 2.2 = 4.4$ MeV

Binding energy of $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ nucleus = $4 \times 7.2 = 28.8$ MeV

Energy released $\Delta E$ = Final binding energy - Initial binding energy

$\Delta E = 28.8 - 4.4 = 24.4$ MeV

Answer: $24.4$

question.text: The energy released when $\dfrac{7}{17.13}$ kg of $^{7}_{3}\text{Li}$ is converted into $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ by proton bombardment is $\alpha \times 10^{32}$ eV. The value of $\alpha$ is _______. (Nearest integer) (Mass of $^{7}_{3}\text{Li} = 7.0183$ u, mass of $^{4}_{2}\text{He} = 4.004$ u, mass of proton $= 1.008$ u and $1$ u $= 931$ MeV/c$^2$ and Avogadro number $= 6.0 \times 10^{23}$)

solution.text:
The nuclear reaction for the proton bombardment of Lithium is:

$^{7}_{3}\text{Li} + ^{1}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow 2 ^{4}_{2}\text{He}$

The mass defect ($\Delta m$) for the reaction is:

$\Delta m = m(^{7}_{3}\text{Li}) + m(^{1}_{1}\text{H}) - 2m(^{4}_{2}\text{He})$

$\Delta m = 7.0183 + 1.008 - 2(4.004)$

$\Delta m = 8.0263 - 8.008 = 0.0183 \text{ u}$

Energy released per reaction ($Q$) is:

$Q = \Delta m \times 931 \text{ MeV} = 0.0183 \times 931 \text{ MeV} = 17.0373 \text{ MeV}$

Number of moles of $^{7}_{3}\text{Li}$ in $\dfrac{7}{17.13} \text{ kg}$:

$n = \dfrac{\dfrac{7}{17.13} \times 10^3 \text{ g}}{7 \text{ g/mol}} = \dfrac{1000}{17.13} \text{ mol}$

Number of atoms of $^{7}_{3}\text{Li}$:

$N = n \times N_A = \dfrac{1000}{17.13} \times 6.0 \times 10^{23} = \dfrac{6}{17.13} \times 10^{26}$

Total energy released ($E$) is:

$E = N \times Q = \left(\dfrac{6}{17.13} \times 10^{26}\right) \times (17.0373 \times 10^6 \text{ eV})$

$E = \dfrac{102.2238}{17.13} \times 10^{32} \text{ eV} \approx 5.967 \times 10^{32} \text{ eV}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we get $\alpha = 6$.

Answer: $6$

question.text:
Assuming the experimental mass of ${}^{12}_{6}C$ as $12\text{ u}$, the mass defect of ${}^{12}_{6}C$ atom is _______ $\text{MeV}/c^2$.
(Mass of proton $= 1.00727\text{ u}$, mass of neutron $= 1.00866\text{ u}$, $1\text{ u} = 931.5\text{ MeV}/c^2$ and $c$ is the speed of the light in vacuum).

solution.text:
The mass of $6$ protons is $6 \times 1.00727\text{ u} = 6.04362\text{ u}$.

The mass of $6$ neutrons is $6 \times 1.00866\text{ u} = 6.05196\text{ u}$.

Total mass of the constituent nucleons is $6.04362\text{ u} + 6.05196\text{ u} = 12.09558\text{ u}$.

The mass defect $\Delta m$ is the difference between the total mass of the nucleons and the experimental mass of the atom (ignoring electron mass as per the given data):

$\Delta m = 12.09558\text{ u} - 12\text{ u} = 0.09558\text{ u}$

Converting the mass defect into $\text{MeV}/c^2$:

$\Delta m = 0.09558 \times 931.5\text{ MeV}/c^2 = 89.03277\text{ MeV}/c^2 \approx 89.03\text{ MeV}/c^2$

Answer: $89.03$

question.text: Two nuclei of mass number $3$ combine with another nucleus of mass number $4$ to yield a nucleus of mass number $10$. If the binding energy per nucleon for the mass numbers $3$, $4$ and $10$ are $5.6$ MeV, $7.4$ MeV and $6.1$ MeV, respectively, then in the process, $\Delta Mc^2 = $ _____ MeV.

solution.text:
The nuclear reaction is given by:

$2 X^{3} + Y^{4} \rightarrow Z^{10}$

The total binding energy of the reactants is the sum of the binding energies of the two nuclei of mass number $3$ and the nucleus of mass number $4$.

Binding energy of reactants $= 2 \times (3 \times 5.6) + (4 \times 7.4)$

$= 33.6 + 29.6 = 63.2$ MeV

The total binding energy of the product nucleus of mass number $10$ is:

Binding energy of product $= 10 \times 6.1 = 61.0$ MeV

The change in mass energy $\Delta M c^2$ is equal to the difference in the total binding energies of the reactants and the product.

$\Delta M c^2 = |63.2 - 61.0| = 2.2$ MeV

Answer: $2.2$

For the nucleus $^{209}_{83}Bi$, the number of protons is $Z = 83$ and the number of neutrons is $N = 209 - 83 = 126$.

Mass of $83$ protons $= 83 \times 1.007825 = 83.649475 \, u$

Mass of $126$ neutrons $= 126 \times 1.008665 = 127.091790 \, u$

Total mass of the nucleons $= 83.649475 + 127.091790 = 210.741265 \, u$

The mass defect $\Delta m$ is given by:

$\Delta m = \text{Total mass of nucleons} - \text{Mass of nucleus}$

$\Delta m = 210.741265 - 208.980388 = 1.760877 \, u$

The total binding energy ($BE$) is:

$BE = \Delta m \times 931 \, \text{MeV}$

$BE = 1.760877 \times 931 = 1639.376 \, \text{MeV}$

The binding energy per nucleon is:

$\dfrac{BE}{A} = \dfrac{1639.376}{209} \approx 7.84 \, \text{MeV}$

Answer: $7.84$

question.text: Two radioactive substances A and B of mass numbers $200$ and $212$ respectively, shows spontaneous $\alpha$-decay with same $Q$ value of $1$ MeV. The ratio of energies of $\alpha$-rays produced by A and B is ________.

solution.text:
In an $\alpha$-decay, the kinetic energy of the emitted $\alpha$-particle is given by the conservation of momentum and energy as:

$K_{\alpha} = \dfrac{A - 4}{A} Q$

where $A$ is the mass number of the parent nucleus.

For substance A ($A = 200$):

$K_{\alpha, A} = \dfrac{200 - 4}{200} Q = \dfrac{196}{200} Q$

For substance B ($A = 212$):

$K_{\alpha, B} = \dfrac{212 - 4}{212} Q = \dfrac{208}{212} Q$

The ratio of the energies of the $\alpha$-rays produced by A and B is:

$\dfrac{K_{\alpha, A}}{K_{\alpha, B}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{196}{200} Q}{\dfrac{208}{212} Q} = \dfrac{196}{200} \times \dfrac{212}{208}$

Simplifying the fractions:

$\dfrac{K_{\alpha, A}}{K_{\alpha, B}} = \dfrac{49}{50} \times \dfrac{53}{52} = \dfrac{2597}{2600}$

question.text: A radioactive nuclei with decay constant $0.5 / \mathrm{s}$ is being produced at a constant rate of 100 nuclei/s. If at $t=0$ there were no nuclei, the time when there are 50 nuclei is:

Let $N$ be the number of nuclei at any time $t$ then,
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{d N}{d t}=100-\lambda N \\
&\text { or } \int_0^N \frac{d N}{(100-\lambda N)}=\int_0^t d t \\
&-\frac{1}{\lambda}[\log (100-\lambda N)]_0^N=t \\
&\log (100-\lambda N)-\log 100=-\lambda t \\
&\log \frac{100-\lambda N}{100}=-\lambda t \\
&\frac{100-\lambda N}{100}=e^{-\lambda t} \\
&1-\frac{\lambda N}{100}=e^{-\lambda t}
\end{aligned}
$$
$$
\begin{aligned}
&N=\frac{100}{\lambda}\left(1-e^{-\lambda} t\right) \\
&\text { As, } N=50 \text { and } \lambda=0.5 / \mathrm{sec} \\
&\therefore 50=\frac{100}{0.5}\left(1-e^{-0.5 t}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$
Solving we get,
$$
t=2 \ln \left(\frac{4}{3}\right) \mathrm{sec}
$$

solution.text:
The number of $^{235}\text{U}$ atoms in 47 g is determined using Avogadro's number.
Molar mass of $^{235}\text{U}$ is 235 g/mol, so the number of moles is $n = 47/235$ mol.
The total number of atoms is $N = (47/235) \times 6 \times 10^{23}$.
Since each fission releases 190 MeV, the total energy released is:

Calculating the numerator: $47 \times 6 \times 190 = 282 \times 190 = 53580$.
Therefore: $E_{total} = \frac{53580}{235} \times 10^{23} = 228 \times 10^{23}$ MeV, giving $\alpha = 228$.

question.text:

question.text:
A nucleus of mass $M+\Delta m$ is at rest and decays into two daughter nuclei of equal mass $\frac{M}{2}$ each. Speed of light is $\mathrm{C}$.
The speed of daughter nuclei is

solution.text:
Conserving the momentum
$$
\begin{gathered}
0=\frac{\mathrm{M}}{2} \mathrm{~V}_1-\frac{\mathrm{M}}{2} \mathrm{~V}_2 \\
\mathrm{~V}_1=\mathrm{V}_2 \quad \quad \ldots \ldots (1) \\
\Delta \mathrm{mc}^2=\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{M}}{2} \mathrm{~V}_1^2+\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{M}}{2} \cdot \mathrm{V}_2^2 \quad \quad \ldots \ldots (2)\\
\Delta \mathrm{mc}^2=\frac{\mathrm{M}}{2} \mathrm{~V}_1^2 \\
\frac{2 \Delta \mathrm{mc}^2}{\mathrm{M}}=\mathrm{V}_1^2 \\
\mathrm{~V}_1=\mathrm{c} \sqrt{\frac{2 \Delta \mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{M}}}
\end{gathered}
$$
